Let's start with two words you'll use all the time. Hardware is the physical parts of a computer, the bits you can touch. Like a keyboard, mouse, processor, monitor or hard disk drive.
Software is the programs and instructions that run on the hardware. Like Windows, Microsoft Word, Google Chrome, or Minecraft.

Every computer system has five parts. Input device, memory, storage, processor and output device.
An input device lets the user put data into a computer. Keyboard, mouse, microphone, webcam, game controller, scanner.
Memory keeps the data that's been input, the software being used and the results of processing, for the short term. It's lost when the computer is turned off. Examples are RAM, ROM and cache memory.
A storage device stores files and installed software for the longer term. Hard disk drive, solid state drive, U S B stick, SD card, DVD, or cloud storage like Google Drive.
The processor processes data according to its instructions, turning it into information. Chips made by Intel, AMD, Apple, or ARM chips in phones.
And an output device lets the user receive information. Monitor, speakers, headphones, printer, projector.
Here's the best tip. Memory is like your desk: what you're working on right now, cleared at the end of the day. Storage is like your schoolbag or locker: kept until you need it again.
And a touchscreen is both input and output. You tap it, that's input, and it shows you pictures, that's output.
Page two. Imagine Mr Butler unscrewing the side of a desktop computer. What would we find?
Some components are internal, inside the case, and some are external, plugged in outside.
The motherboard is the main circuit board. Every other component plugs into it so they can communicate. Think of it as the town where everyone lives.
The C P U is the processor, or the brain. It carries out the instructions of programs and does the calculations.
RAM is memory that holds the programs and data being used right now, so the C P U can get them quickly. It's wiped when the power goes off.
The hard disk drive is storage. It keeps the operating system, programs and your files when the power is off.
Many newer computers use an S S D instead. It has no moving parts, so it's faster, quieter and tougher.
The power supply changes mains electricity from the wall socket into the low voltages the components need.
The graphics card has its own processor, the G P U, and its own memory, to create the images, video and game graphics sent to the monitor.
The fan unit and heat sink keep the C P U cool so it doesn't overheat. And the chassis is the case that holds and protects everything.
Outside, the keyboard, mouse, webcam and microphone are input devices, and the monitor is an output device.
And a warning: never open a computer while it's plugged in. The power supply carries mains electricity.

Page five: algorithms. An algorithm is a sequence of instructions, or a set of rules, followed to complete a task or solve a problem.
The instructions must be clear, short and specific. A recipe for a cake is an algorithm. So are directions to a place.
But computers don't understand algorithms written in English. An algorithm has to be translated into code, in a programming language like Scratch, Python or C sharp.

And the order matters. Putting instructions in the right order creates a sequence. Crossing a zebra crossing with an island: look right first, cross to the island, stop, then look left before the second half.
Or making a cuppa. You could add sugar before milk, so there isn't only one correct sequence. But you can't pour the tea before you've added the water.
And there's a fun river puzzle. A man and a woman weigh a hundred kilograms each, two children weigh fifty each, and the boat holds a hundred kilograms. How do they all cross?
The children do the shuttling, because they're the only ones who can travel together. It takes nine crossings.
Page six: flowcharts. A flowchart shows an algorithm using symbols joined by arrows. There are four main symbols.
Start and Stop is a rounded rectangle. Input or Output is a parallelogram, that's a slanted box.
Process is a plain rectangle, for an instruction like wait five minutes. And Decision is a diamond, which asks a yes or no question.
Test yourself. Which flowchart symbol is the only one with two exits?
The decision diamond. One exit for Yes and one for No.
In the bath example, the decision asks: is the bath full? If no, the arrow loops back to wait five minutes again. If yes, turn off the taps and enjoy the bath.
So a No arrow that loops back makes steps repeat. And every flowchart needs exactly one Start and at least one Stop.
Page seven: computer control versus human control. Who's better at running a junction, traffic lights or a police officer?
Computers don't need breaks, sick days or pay. They repeat actions identically forever, work in dangerous places, process sensor data quickly, and manage thousands of inputs at once.
But they're only as good as their programming, which may contain errors. They don't know what to do in situations they weren't programmed for. They rely on power. And they can cost a lot.
So for a busy junction in Enniskillen, traffic lights handle normal traffic every day. But in a crash or a power cut, a police officer is better, because people can think and adapt.
Page eight: binary. Computers understand a very simple language: just zeros and ones. That's called binary.
Each zero or one is like a tiny switch, off or on. Everything on your phone, photos, songs, messages, is stored as huge patterns of zeros and ones.
Now, variables. A variable is a location in memory where you can temporarily store text or numbers.
It's like an empty box with a label on it. You choose the variable name, and your program can change what's inside.

Fifty-five. It takes what's in X, adds five, and puts the answer back in X.

And variables make programs reusable. A program that always works out two times four always prints eight. Not very useful.

Then there are data types. A data type tells the computer what kind of data a value is. There are five to know.
Integer, a whole number, like fifteen or minus four. Double, a number with a decimal point, like three point one four.
String, which is text, like Hello E R G S. Character, a single letter or symbol. And Boolean, which is true or false.
Your phone number should be stored as a string, not an integer. It starts with a zero, and you never do maths with it.
Last page: selection and loops. Selection uses an IF statement. Code inside the IF only runs if the condition is true.
And ELSE gives the code to run when the condition is false. If my value equals ten, show a tick, else show a cross. Only one of the two ever runs.
A loop means to repeat, also called iteration. There are two types.
A count-controlled loop, or for loop, repeats a set number of times, like repeat four times.
A condition-controlled loop, or while loop, repeats as long as a condition is true.
Last test. My value starts at seven. While my value is less than ten, add one. How many times does the loop run?
Three times. Seven becomes eight, eight becomes nine, nine becomes ten. Then ten is not less than ten, so it stops.
Top tip: do you know how many times? Yes means count-controlled. No means condition-controlled.
